READING

**Setting up the comparison**

The central question is which course puts more money in Thistledown's hands over the relevant horizon and at what risk. I will strip out the sunk cost (the £187,000 spent in 2024 is gone either way) and work purely on future cash flows.

**Establishing per-colony honey yield**

£143,000 across 640 colonies = £223.44 per colony per season.
The problem identifies borage (Kirkhallow) as the crop the 400 Vantwyn colonies miss, at £71 per colony. It does not identify heather as a missed crop—the colonies come out of the orchards too late for borage, implying they are back in time for the heather flush in August/September. So heather yield per colony ≈ £223.44 − £71 = £152.44.

**The incremental case for Vantwyn, per season**

For the 400 colonies diverted to Vantwyn, the gain over keeping them on honey is:

| Item | £ |
|---|---|
| Pollination income (400 × £168) | +67,200 |
| Borage foregone (400 × £71) | −28,400 |
| Spray replacement (400 × 9% = 36 colonies × £210) | −7,560 |
| Haulage and labour | −6,900 |
| **Net incremental gain per season** | **+24,340** |

This exactly matches the problem's own framing ("£67,200 a season, against the borage those colonies give up, the 9 per cent the spray programme takes and the haulage"), which is reassuring.

Note: the 36 colonies that die from the spray programme may not contribute a full heather crop in the season they die. If their heather contribution is largely lost, the true net falls below £24,340—perhaps by 36 × £152.44 = £5,488, reducing it to around £18,850. The £24,340 is therefore the optimistic ceiling, not a floor.

**Three-season totals**

At the optimistic ceiling:
- Incremental operating advantage of TREVANNOCK over three seasons: 3 × £24,340 = **£73,020**

**The equipment pivot**

| | ORMSCLEUCH | TREVANNOCK |
|---|---|---|
| Equipment proceeds | £96,000, received now (before Nov 2026) | ~£20,000 for the lorry only, realised after the 2029 season |
| Timing | Certain, immediate | Three years away, and only the lorry is priced; pallet value post-2029 is unspecified |

Equipment advantage to ORMSCLEUCH (face value): £96,000 − £20,000 = **£76,000**

Even without discounting, £76,000 > £73,020. ORMSCLEUCH is ahead by roughly £3,000 on raw figures.

**Time value tightens the case further**

The £96,000 is in hand now (late 2026). The TREVANNOCK operating surplus of £24,340 arrives in three annual instalments (2027–2029), and the £20,000 residual arrives in late 2029 or 2030. At a modest 5 % annual discount rate:

- PV of three annual instalments of £24,340: £23,181 + £22,078 + £21,025 = **£66,284**
- PV of £20,000 in four years: **£16,454**

Total PV of TREVANNOCK's future advantage: £66,284 + £16,454 = £82,738
ORMSCLEUCH gives £96,000 now.

ORMSCLEUCH is ahead by roughly **£13,000 in present-value terms** even at the optimistic ceiling for TREVANNOCK's operating surplus—and the gap widens if spray mortality bites into the heather crop.

**Checking the strategic upside of TREVANNOCK**

Two arguments are made for TREVANNOCK beyond the numbers:

1. *Coldharbour and Nyefield are asking for 2028 rates.* These are real prospects, but they carry no attached figure and no commitment. With 400 colonies already pledged to Vantwyn, Thistledown would have only the remaining 240 home colonies to offer, and those are the heather and borage workers. Taking more migratory work without adding colonies would cannibalise the honey crop further. To serve additional vale growers at any meaningful scale, Thistledown would need to expand colony numbers or acquire a new LEZ-compliant lorry before 2030—costs the scenario does not budget.

2. *Staying in the vale keeps options open.* True, but none of the three original contracts that justified buying the kit has renewed. The market has already signalled a retreat once. Unquantified optionality is not worth a certain £76,000 in equipment proceeds when the three-year operating arithmetic barely reaches £73,000 even under favourable assumptions.

**Risk audit**

| Risk | ORMSCLEUCH | TREVANNOCK |
|---|---|---|
| Spray losses | None | 9 % certain; possibly higher |
| Equipment value erosion | None (sold now) | LEZ permit gone 2030; equipment stranded in vale without replacement |
| Colony health (migratory stress) | None | Real but unquantified |
| Revenue concentration | Honey-only | Slightly more diversified, but pollination income thin |
| Operational complexity | One business | Two operations, haulage logistics |

TREVANNOCK carries more risk in every category that is quantifiable.

**Sunk-cost note**

The £187,000 spent in 2024 and the queen-rearing shed (not part of the Ravensgate offer) are irrelevant to the forward decision. The shed stays either way; it can contribute to routine colony replacement under ORMSCLEUCH as well.

**Summary**

The arithmetic resolves cleanly: the maximum three-season operating surplus from Vantwyn (£73,020, optimistic) is smaller than the equipment value sacrificed by declining the Ravensgate offer (£76,000, face value), and the gap widens to roughly £13,000 once the timing difference is discounted. The strategic upside (Coldharbour, Nyefield) is unpriced and would require further investment to exploit. ORMSCLEUCH delivers a certain £96,000 now, eliminates spray mortality, and reduces the business to its proven, simpler core.

---

CALL
ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
The certain, immediate Ravensgate proceeds of £96,000 exceed the maximum three-season incremental operating surplus that Vantwyn can produce (£73,020 at best) even before discounting, and every quantifiable risk—spray mortality, LEZ permit expiry, operational complexity—falls on the TREVANNOCK side.
